title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Ava Patel
body:
Summary:

This consolidated reference defines Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding conventions, infrastructure, model-serving best practices, observability, and performance targets. It includes ADR templates and an ADR log for decisions that affect cross-team architecture. Use this doc as the canonical starting point for new services, model onboarding, and infra changes.

1) Purpose and scope

- Purpose: provide a single, opinionated set of standards to keep service design predictable, secure, and observable while enabling high-throughput, low-latency LLM inference.
- Scope: applies to all services and components owned by engineering teams that interact with the Redwood runtime, internal control planes, Dedicated control plane, or Private deployment packages.

2) API standards (REST + gRPC + design guidelines)

Intro: our public and internal APIs must be consistent, versioned, discoverable, and backward-compatible where feasible. The following rules apply to both hosted and private control plane APIs.

Core rules:
- Resource-oriented URLs: prefer nouns, hierarchical structure, and plural resources. Example: POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/models/{model_id}/invocations
- Versioning: include major version in path (e.g., /v1/). Use semantic versioning for implementation releases.
- Idempotency: all mutate operations must be idempotent when feasible (idempotency-key header for long-running jobs).
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination (next_cursor token) for lists that can grow indefinitely.
- Error model: use consistent error envelope with top-level fields: code (string), message (string), details (optional array). Map HTTP codes to standard behaviors (400 bad request, 401 unauthorized, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 rate limit, 500+ server).
- Throttling/Rate limits: expose per-route X-RateLimit* headers and return Retry-After on 429.
- Authentication: all APIs require mTLS where traffic crosses trust boundaries and OAuth2 bearer tokens for user-scoped calls. Service-to-service calls should prefer short-lived workload identity tokens.
- Streaming: follow chunked Transfer-Encoding for HTTP streaming responses; include an explicit end-of-stream marker and per-chunk event types (data, progress, error).

API example (curl):

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/projects/abcd/models/llama-2-13b/invocations \
  -d '{"input":"Summarize the following...","options":{"max_tokens":256}}'

3) Coding standards and repository conventions

- Languages: primary languages in services are Go (runtime/infra), Python (evals, tooling), TypeScript (console, SDKs).
- Formatting: go fmt/goimports for Go; black + ruff for Python; Prettier + ESLint for TypeScript. CI must fail on formatting/lint errors.
- Typing: enable go vet and enable mypy (strictness level: --strict) for Python services that are customer-facing. TypeScript projects must use --noImplicitAny.
- Dependencies: require Dependabot or equivalent for automated dependency updates and SCA scanning enabled. Major version upgrades must use an ADR if public API changes occur.
- Monorepo guidance: keep service boundaries clear, use minimal shared packages (platform libs only) and publish clear CHANGELOG.md for shared packages.
- Tests: unit tests (>= 80% coverage for core logic), integration tests that run against a hermetic test runtime or local mock. End-to-end tests for critical flows (invocation path, auth, billing) required before major releases.

CI example (snippet):
- Steps: checkout, lint, fmt-check, unit-test, integration-test (parallel where possible), build artifact, scan, publish to staging.

4) Infrastructure standards

Ownership and naming:
- Kubernetes clusters: names must include environment and region (e.g., redwood-prod-us-west1).
- Terraform modules: central modules live in infra/terraform-modules with module README, inputs, outputs, and changelog.

Security and networking:
- All external ingress terminates at edge gateways with WAF. Internal services communicate over private VPCs with mTLS.
- Secrets: use customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. No hard-coded secrets in code.
- IAM: least-privilege roles and short-lived credentials by default.

Capacity & deployments:
- Autoscaling policies: target CPU/latency-based autoscaling for control-plane components; for Dedicated runtime GPU pools, autoscaler uses queue-depth and tail-latency signals.
- Deployment: all services use canary rollouts by default with 10% traffic for 15 min, automatic rollback on error rate > 0.5% or p95 latency regression > 20%.

5) Model-serving standards

Goal: maximize throughput while preserving per-request latency SLOs and output quality.

Model packaging and versions:
- Model artifacts must include metadata: model_id, architecture, tokenizer_version, quantization_profile, kv_cache_compat_version. Store manifest as model.manifest.json.
- Versioning: immutable model releases with semantic version in manifest (e.g., 2025-11-llama-2-13b-v1).

Execution constraints:
- Supported runtimes: CPU for small models (<2B), GPU for >2B; quantized builds must explicitly declare supported hardware.
- KV cache policy: shared KV caches allowed for batched requests; eviction must be LRU with per-customer isolation in Dedicated deployments.

Quality gates & evals:
- Every production model must include a baseline eval suite (prompt sets + metrics) and a rollout gate: no rollout beyond 10% traffic until key quality metrics (ROUGE/accuracy/semantic-similarity) pass baseline.
- Regression monitoring: automated weekly evals and alerting on >5% relative drop in key metric.

Autoscaling and fallback:
- Router policies: route by latency target, cost tier, region, model compatibility. If capacity constrained, router will fallback to a compatible quantized variant or lower-tier model according to policy.

6) Observability standards

Instrumentation:
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry with distributed tracing enabled across all RPC boundaries. Root spans created on public API ingress.
- Metrics: Prometheus metrics with standardized labels: service, route, model_id, customer_tier, region.
- Logs: structured JSON logs (timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, msg, fields). Logs forwarded to centralized ELK/observability platform with 30-day retention for infra, 90-day for security events by default.

Dashboard & alerts:
- Dashboards: per-service and per-model dashboards (latency histograms, QPS, errors, cost/token).
- Alerting thresholds (default):
  - Error budget burn: page at 5% burn in 1 hour, escalate at 20% burn in 1 hour.
  - P95 latency: page if p95 > SLO + 25% for 5m.
  - Error rate: page on sustained error rate > 0.5% for 5m.

Logs and traces retention:
- Traces: keep sampling of 100% for 1h, 10% for 7d, 1% for 30d.
- Logs: index errors at ingest; keep debug-level logs only for 3 days unless flagged.

7) Performance standards and SLOs

Global SLOs (examples — adjust per-service SLA):
- Control plane API (hosted): 99.9% availability monthly.
- Model invocation latency (small models <=2B): p95 < 200ms, p99 < 450ms.
- Model invocation latency (large models >2B): p95 < 600ms, p99 < 1200ms.
- Error rate: customer-facing endpoints < 0.2% 5xx errors.

Cost-performance levers:
- Batching: prefer dynamic batching for high QPS routes with configurable max_batch_size and max_hold_ms (defaults: 32 tokens, 50ms).
- Quantization profiles: specify quantization_profile in model manifest; default recommendations made by Redwood Optimize analysis.

Perf engineering process:
- Benchmarking harness: every model onboarding must run the standard benchmarking suite (latency, throughput, memory) across target hardware. Results stored in model-perf/{model_id}/{date}.csv and linked in model manifest.
- Regression triage: guardrail alerts trigger a regression triage runbook (see section 9).

8) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process and templates

- When to write an ADR: any cross-team architectural change, public API change, or infra change that affects SLOs, cost, or security.
- ADR required approvals: author + owner_team lead + infra/security reviewer + one architect reviewer.

ADR template (use this exact structure):
- ADR ID: ADR-YYYY-NNN
- Title: short descriptive title
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded
- Context: background and constraints
- Decision: chosen approach and rationale
- Alternatives considered: list alternatives and brief pros/cons
- Consequences: operational, cost, and migration impact
- Rollout plan: canary steps and rollback criteria
- Owner: person/team responsible
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD

Example ADR (short):
- ADR ID: ADR-2025-014
- Title: Use cursor-based pagination for model listing APIs
- Status: accepted
- Context: model lists can be large for enterprise customers and offset pagination is inefficient at scale.
- Decision: adopt cursor-based pagination and return opaque next_cursor tokens.
- Alternatives: offset-based pagination (rejected for scale), page-token (same as cursor).
- Consequences: small client changes; servers must maintain stable ordering for determinism.

9) Runbooks and regression triage (brief)

Runbook triggers:
- Performance regression alert (p95 increase or cost-per-token spike).
- Quality regression alert (>5% drop on key eval metric).

Short triage steps (performance regression):
1. Confirm alert in dashboard and query traces for impacted routes.
2. Identify recent deploys or config changes in last 24h (terraform, rollout).
3. Reproduce in benchmark harness; collect flamegraphs and device-level metrics.
4. Apply mitigation: reduce batch size, cold-start warmup, pin to previous model variant, or rollback canary.
5. Postmortem: within 48h, include impact, root cause, and permanent fix.

10) Ownership, governance, and exceptions

- Governance: architecture council (members: platform architects + eng leads) meets weekly to review ADRs and high-impact changes.
- Exceptions: temporary exceptions require an ADR with temporary status and an explicit expiration date.
- Ownership: each service must list a single on-call owner and a primary code owner team in CODEOWNERS.

Appendices

A) Example model.manifest.json (snippet):
{
  "model_id": "llama-2-13b-redwood-v1",
  "architecture": "decoder-only",
  "tokenizer_version": "2025-09",
  "quantization_profile": "int8",
  "kv_cache_compat_version": "v2",
  "perf_artifact": "s3://model-perf/llama-2-13b/2026-01-12/summary.csv"
}

B) ADR index (recent entries):
- ADR-2025-001: Auth model for control-plane -> accepted
- ADR-2025-014: Cursor-based pagination for model listing -> accepted
- ADR-2025-030: Default batching policy for runtime -> accepted

C) Quick checklist for new service onboarding:
- Add service to CODEOWNERS and declare on-call rotation.
- Create API contract (OpenAPI or proto) and place in apis/{service}.yaml.
- Wire OpenTelemetry traces and export to central collector.
- Add Prometheus metrics and dashboards.
- Add CI checks: lint, format, unit tests, integration smoke.
- Add deployment Terraform module and run infra review.
- Create ADR if public API or infra change is required.
